The Beta Function

The area under a curve shaped by two exponents, p and q, is the beta function. Sliders morph the curve's shape.

The two ends of the curve are pulled with different strengths. So the hump shifts and changes height. This area equals an exact ratio of gamma functions.

For example, pull the two ends of a 🧵 string with different strengths and the bulge in the middle changes shape. Adjusting the end pulls is what p and q do.

B(p,q)=∫01tp−1(1−t)q−1 dt(p,q>0)B(p,q)=\int_0^1 t^{p-1}(1-t)^{q-1}\,dt\quad(p,q>0)B(p,q)=∫01​tp−1(1−t)q−1dt(p,q>0)
B(p,q)=Γ(p)Γ(q)Γ(p+q)B(p,q)=\frac{\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)}{\Gamma(p+q)}B(p,q)=Γ(p+q)Γ(p)Γ(q)​

A note (an idea-level sketch, not a proof): the bridge to the gamma function, B(p,q)=Γ(p)Γ(q)Γ(p+q)B(p,q) = \frac{\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)}{\Gamma(p+q)}B(p,q)=Γ(p+q)Γ(p)Γ(q)​, follows the standard sketch — write Γ(p)Γ(q)\Gamma(p)\Gamma(q)Γ(p)Γ(q) as a double integral over (0,∞)2(0,\infty)^2(0,∞)2; the polar substitution t=r2sin⁡2θt = r^2\sin^2\thetat=r2sin2θ, s=r2cos⁡2θs = r^2\cos^2\thetas=r2cos2θ then separates the radial part into Γ(p+q)\Gamma(p+q)Γ(p+q) and the angular part into B(p,q)B(p,q)B(p,q). The full justification, including Fubini's theorem on the unbounded domain, goes beyond this scene, so we take the relation as the bridge, not as a proved theorem here.
